{"task": {"id": "I_kwDOVRkquM8AAAABiCRjlg", "item_id": "PVTI_lAHOAHSLSM4Bn_T5zhLaDvM", "project_id": "PVT_kwHOAHSLSM4Bn_T5", "number": 174, "title": "Benchmark against established SNES emulators and iteratively optimize toward competitive performance", "body": "## Goal

Make snes-rust substantially faster through **competitive benchmarking and repeated, evidence-driven optimization**, not a one-off micro-optimization. Continue profiling, implementing, measuring, and reviewing changes until performance is reasonably close to established SNES emulators on comparable workloads, or a concrete remaining limitation is demonstrated and tracked for continued work.

The latest inspected baseline is `main` at `416b6c4097c447cd2f2a58298c153ab6295f243a` (PR #171). The repository already has a native release runner (`snes-run`), a production Rust/Wasm browser build, real ROM fixtures and correctness tests. Use those rather than treating UI FPS alone as a benchmark.

## 1. Research and run reference emulators

Start by surveying credible, maintained SNES emulators, their execution models, accuracy tradeoffs, licenses, supported workloads and available native/browser builds. Select practical references and **actually run them** on the development machine. Native applications are valid reference targets, not just web emulators.

Initial candidates (not a predetermined ranking or exhaustive list):

- [Snes9x](https://github.com/snes9xgit/snes9x) or the [current libretro Snes9x core](https://docs.libretro.com/library/snes9x/) as a practical, optimized reference; consider native and equivalent WebAssembly builds of the same core, where feasible.
- [ares](https://github.com/ares-emulator/ares) / bsnes as an accuracy-oriented reference for interpreting the costs of more detailed emulation.
- Other maintained browser SNES emulators or native cores if they provide useful controlled measurements.

Use at least one actual native reference and, if feasible, a comparable browser/Wasm reference. Pin versions/build flags and document why each comparison is meaningful. Use current, reasonably accurate configurations, not old speed-hack variants as an unquestioned correctness target. Do not merely collect advertised FPS or published benchmark numbers from unrelated hardware.

Study source and architecture of faster reference implementations, subject to licenses. snes-rust is MIT-licensed; do not copy incompatible/noncommercial/GPL implementation code into it. Use independently implemented optimizations, documenting references and preserving licensing/provenance.

## 2. Establish reproducible baselines

The implementer should look for usable ROMs in their own development workspace, nearby relevant ROM-development directories and existing test ROM paths. The repository already has bundled Shionari/Yonaki and source-built diagnostics/cleared fixtures; the README describes optional local ROM paths, including `GOTHICVANIA_ROM` and `CASTLE_ROM`. Use available, legally obtained/authorized ROMs locally, including real games where possible. Do not request ROM uploads from the maintainer unnecessarily; do not search unrelated private directories, obtain unauthorized ROMs, commit redistributable-uncleared ROMs, or publish their contents. Record workload identifiers/hashes and reproducible input sequences, not ROM bytes. Use repository fixtures as a fallback if other local ROMs are unavailable.

Benchmark multiple representative ordinary NTSC LoROM/HiROM workloads, with CPU-heavy gameplay, sprites/background rendering, DMA/HDMA, audio/DSP, and typical real gameplay. Include at least the bundled demos and appropriate diagnostics or other playable ROMs; include hires/Mode 7 where supported. Avoid using only title screens, idle loops or a single convenient ROM. Verify the workload is actually running correctly in both emulators, using equivalent reset state, frame/field counts, input sequences and audio/video work.

Measure:

- Native optimized release core vs optimized native reference (e.g. comparable headless/libretro frame loop with video/audio generation enabled).
- Production optimized Wasm core vs Wasm reference when feasible; isolate Wasm/JS and browser overhead from the core rather than attributing all native-vs-browser differences to emulator architecture.
- Full browser playback, Pixel and CRT separately, with realistic viewport/DPR and audio enabled; include mobile/low-power conditions if available. If emulated throttling is used, label it separately from real-device results.
- Uncapped throughput (emulated frames/fields per second, ms per emulated frame, real-time speed multiple); real-time frame pacing (median and p95/p99 frame time, missed frame deadlines, audio underruns), CPU usage, memory and any meaningful startup/load costs. Measure actual guest progression, not rAF callback count or nominal 60fps alone.
- Same host/OS/architecture, comparable release optimizations, output/accuracy settings, fixed workload lengths, warm-up, repeated trials and variability. Avoid vsync, audio sync, frame caps, debug logging, run-ahead, rewind, frameskip and fast-forward differences confounding the uncapped comparison; confirm native and Wasm builds perform the same relevant work. Clearly disclose non-equivalent settings and accuracy/features. Do not compare throttled browser 60fps against native uncapped throughput as if directly equivalent.

Create a lightweight repeatable benchmark harness, or extend the existing native runner and browser test infrastructure. Keep benchmark execution separate from ordinary mandatory correctness tests; avoid making CI slow or adding fragile wall-clock thresholds to shared runners. Document machine, tool versions, build flags, commands, ROM hashes, frame windows, and raw/summary results in a dedicated performance report.

## 3. Analyze and iterate

For each substantial measured performance gap:

1. Profile snes-rust (native and Wasm where appropriate) with representative workloads and break down time by subsystem.
2. Investigate how the faster reference handles the corresponding workload: architecture, event scheduling, rendering, memory access and dispatch, batching, caching, compiler choices, etc. Where meaningful, inspect/profile the reference itself.
3. Propose concrete candidate optimizations, prioritize by measured impact and risk, and **implement** promising ones rather than stopping at a research report.
4. Run correctness tests and repeat the same benchmark after each meaningful change; record before/after speed, regression risk, and reasons for rejected approaches.
5. Reprofile the new baseline, identify the next bottleneck, and continue the loop.

Likely investigation areas (hypotheses, not requirements to optimize all of them): 65C816/SPC700 dispatch and bus mapping, per-cycle/timing/scheduler costs and DMA/HDMA, PPU raster/tile/sprite/color math and memory access, DSP/audio mixing and buffering, allocations/copies/format conversions, native vs Wasm compiler/codegen, JS/Wasm boundary and framebuffer uploads, CRT rendering, and browser frame/audio scheduling.

Prefer simple, maintainable, measured optimizations. Preserve hardware-visible behavior, ordering, timing, output and supported features; do not make the emulator look faster by running fewer emulated cycles, skipping rendering/audio, reducing accuracy, or silently selecting Pixel instead of CRT. No game-specific speed hacks or brittle ROM-specific shortcuts. Validate intermediate output, guest state and deterministic input replay where applicable. Avoid unsafe code or extra abstractions without a measured and justified benefit.

## Completion criteria — competitive performance, not one optimization

This is an iterative performance initiative. **Do not close merely because one bottleneck was optimized, one benchmark improved, or a single PR merged.** Multiple focused PRs and checkpoint commits are encouraged so useful improvements can land incrementally.

- [ ] Establish the baseline/reference suite and a measured performance target before optimizing. As a practical initial target, aim for **at least 80% of the throughput of the selected practical optimized reference** on representative comparable workloads (equivalently, no more than 1.25× its time per emulated frame), in native-to-native and Wasm-to-Wasm comparisons where available. Use the same target/settings throughout; document any genuinely non-comparable accuracy/architecture/host overhead. This is an engineering target, not a claim of current performance.
- [ ] Target consistently sustainable real-time browser NTSC gameplay with useful frame-time headroom and stable audio in supported Pixel and CRT configurations on the stated test devices. Record worst representative workloads and avoid hiding material regressions behind an average.
- [ ] Investigate every material residual gap, including major outlier workloads, with profiles and reference-emulator research. If still materially slower, continue the profile/optimize/verify cycle, prioritize the next improvement, and keep this initiative open. Do not redefine the benchmark or choose a slower reference just to declare success.
- [ ] If a target is genuinely blocked by necessary accuracy, intrinsic platform overhead, unavailable tooling, or another evidenced constraint, quantify the residual gap, explain the tradeoff, record concrete next experiments/linked tasks, and keep unresolved performance work explicitly visible. Do not substitute an unverified claim of parity for measurements. If a different target is warranted, explain it with evidence for maintainer review.
- [ ] Preserve correctness: all applicable Rust tests, CPU/SPC700/HDMA and other existing diagnostic checks, real-game replay and browser/Pages integration tests, audio, SRAM and local cartridge library, Pixel/CRT, fullscreen and input behavior. Compare real outputs/state at fixed inputs; do not weaken assertions or bypass CI.
- [ ] Publish an auditable baseline-versus-final performance table for snes-rust and each reference, per workload/build, with relative ratios, frame pacing/audio results, measurements, implemented changes, remaining bottlenecks and actionable proposals. Include reproducible commands and any limitations. No fabricated test or benchmark results.

## Workflow

Follow the repository's Issue → PR → review → merge process and existing [test/CI performance principles](https://github.com/takahirox/snes-rust/blob/main/docs/development-flow.md#test-and-ci-performance-principles). Maintain the benchmark report and progress checklist across PRs, linking them here. Use narrowly scoped PRs for individual optimizations rather than an unreviewable rewrite; keep the umbrella issue open until the overall measured goal is met. Do not add automatic closing keywords for the umbrella on an intermediate PR. Independent external-tool transport failures (#159) or intermittent CRT test failures (#157) must be identified separately, not used to excuse performance regressions or skip validation.

After each merge that changes production behavior, check the corresponding Pages deployment and actual published app as appropriate; report verified results and track confirmed regressions separately. This is post-merge verification, not a pre-merge condition. No background monitoring is implied.
